data.sourcePassage:
King John ruled England from 1199 to 1216. He inherited an expensive kingdom and faced problems that would have challenged any medieval ruler, but his own decisions made things much worse. In 1204, he lost Normandy to the French king Philip II. Normandy mattered deeply because it had been connected to English kings since 1066, and many English barons had family lands and interests there. Losing it made John look weak and cost him political support.

To try to recover Normandy, John raised heavy taxes, including a feudal payment called scutage. Many barons resented paying large amounts of money for campaigns that repeatedly failed. In 1214, John's allies were defeated at the Battle of Bouvines in France. This convinced many barons that John was not just unlucky but genuinely incompetent. Meanwhile, John had also quarrelled with Pope Innocent III, leading to England being placed under an interdict in 1208 and John being excommunicated in 1209. Although John made peace with the Pope in 1213, these events had damaged his reputation as a Christian king.

By 1215, a group of rebel barons had organised and taken London. They forced John to agree to a document at Runnymede in June 1215 — Magna Carta, the Great Charter. Magna Carta included many clauses. Some dealt with practical matters such as inheritance payments, debts, and the use of royal courts. Others became famous over time, especially the promise that justice should not be sold, delayed, or denied, and that certain payments should need common counsel.

However, Magna Carta was not an immediate success. John asked Pope Innocent III to annul it, which he did. Civil war followed. John died in 1216, and Magna Carta was reissued several times under his young son Henry III, partly to gain political support. In the short term it failed to bring peace, but in the long term it became a powerful symbol of the idea that even kings must obey the law.

questions.question: Why did King John lose political support when he lost Normandy in 1204?
options: Because Normandy was the location of the English Parliament
Because many English barons had family lands and interests there, and losing it made John look weak
Because Normandy was where the Pope lived
Because it meant John could no longer collect scutage

questions.question: What was the Battle of Bouvines in 1214?
options: A battle where John defeated the barons
A battle where John's allies were defeated in France, convincing barons he was incompetent
The battle that ended Magna Carta
A battle between England and Scotland
questions.modelAnswer: The Battle of Bouvines in 1214 was a defeat for John's allies in France. It convinced many barons that John was incompetent and had wasted their money on failed campaigns.

questions.question: What does the passage say about Magna Carta's immediate effect in 1215?
options: It immediately brought peace and was accepted by all sides
It failed to bring immediate peace — John had it annulled and civil war followed
It created modern democracy right away
It gave all English people equal rights

questions.question: According to the passage, what was the long-term significance of Magna Carta?
options: It immediately ended baronial rebellion
It created Parliament in 1215
It became a powerful symbol of the idea that even kings must obey the law
It gave the Pope control over English kingship

data.sourcePassage:
Parliament did not appear fully formed in one year or because of one person. It grew slowly from royal councils over several centuries. In the early medieval period, kings regularly called together powerful nobles and Church leaders to seek advice, discuss national matters, and sometimes gain approval for new taxes. These councils were the starting point for Parliament.

Magna Carta itself contributed to the idea that certain payments needed common counsel — that is, agreement from an important group of people before the king could demand money. This was not modern democracy, but it planted the idea that taxation required some form of consent.

Henry III, who became king as a child in 1216, continued to face pressure from barons who wanted more say in royal government. In 1258, barons forced him to accept the Provisions of Oxford, which tried to make government more accountable to a council of barons. Henry eventually resisted and civil war followed.

Simon de Montfort, who led the baronial opposition, defeated Henry III at the Battle of Lewes in 1264. In 1265, de Montfort called a Parliament that included not only nobles and clergy but also two knights from each shire and two burgesses from each borough. This was significant because it brought wider representation into the political arena. However, de Montfort was defeated and killed at the Battle of Evesham later in 1265, and his Parliament did not continue directly.

Edward I, who became king in 1272, used Parliament more regularly. In 1295, he called what later became known as the Model Parliament, which included archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, barons, knights, and burgesses. Edward needed taxation for his wars in Wales, Scotland, and France. By consulting a wider group, he gained support and made taxation seem more legitimate. The Model Parliament became an important example because it showed what a broader Parliament could look like.

data.sourceTitle: Why Did Barons Challenge Royal Power?
data.targetTitle: Why Did Barons Challenge Royal Power?
data.sourcePassage:
Medieval barons did not rebel against kings simply because they were greedy or disloyal. They challenged royal power when they believed the king had broken the accepted rules of medieval government. To understand why barons sometimes rebelled, it helps to understand how medieval kingship was supposed to work.

A medieval king was expected to fulfil certain duties: defend the kingdom, protect the Church, provide justice, listen to wise advice, and respect established customs about how money was raised. A king was very powerful, but his power was supposed to come with responsibilities. If he ignored these responsibilities, powerful nobles could argue that he was not ruling as a proper king.

Barons held land from the king and owed military service and loyalty in return. This relationship was built on mutual obligation. Barons were expected to support the king, but they expected the king to respect their rights, protect their property, and govern fairly. When kings like John raised money in ways barons saw as arbitrary or unjust, sold justice, took hostages, or exploited feudal customs harshly, barons felt their side of the bargain was being broken.

It is important not to see the barons as early democrats trying to create freedom for everyone. Their demands in Magna Carta were mostly about protecting the rights of barons, free men, and the Church — not ordinary peasants or the poor. Many of Magna Carta's clauses protected elite interests.

However, over the long term, the principle that even a king must follow rules and respect custom became more widely useful. Later generations — lawyers, Parliamentarians, and reformers — used Magna Carta and the memory of baronial resistance to argue for broader limits on royal power. In this way, a document created to protect barons became a foundation for wider ideas about law and rights.

questions.question: According to the passage, why did barons challenge royal power?
options: Simply because they were greedy and disloyal
Because they wanted to replace the king with a president
When they believed the king had broken accepted rules of medieval government
Because they wanted to abolish the Church
questions.modelAnswer: Barons challenged royal power when they believed the king had broken the accepted rules of medieval government — such as respecting their rights, governing fairly, and not raising money arbitrarily.

questions.question: What does the passage say barons expected from a king in return for their loyalty?
options: Complete freedom from all taxes
The right to become king themselves
That the king would respect their rights, protect their property, and govern fairly
That the king would never go to war
questions.modelAnswer: Barons expected the king to respect their rights, protect their property, and govern fairly. This was the mutual obligation at the heart of the relationship between king and barons.

questions.question: The passage warns against seeing the barons as 'early democrats'. Why?
options: Because barons never used written documents
Because their demands mainly protected elite interests — barons, free men, and the Church — not ordinary people
Because they supported King John throughout
Because they never challenged royal power
questions.modelAnswer: The barons were not early democrats because their demands mainly protected their own interests and those of free men and the Church. Ordinary peasants and the poor gained little directly from Magna Carta.

questions.question: How does the passage explain that Magna Carta became more significant over time than it was in 1215?
options: Because it was immediately popular with all people including peasants
Because later lawyers, Parliamentarians, and reformers used it to argue for broader limits on royal power
Because John kept all its promises after signing it
Because Edward I abolished it and replaced it with something better
questions.modelAnswer: Magna Carta became more significant over time because later generations — lawyers, Parliamentarians, and reformers — used it and the memory of baronial resistance to argue for broader limits on royal power, turning a baronial document into a foundation for wider ideas about law and rights.
